title: Cannabis Allergy: Symptoms, Triggers and What to Do
h1: Allergic to Weed? Signs, Triggers and Next Steps
metaDescription: Cannabis allergy explained: symptoms from smoke, touch or food, anaphylaxis warning signs, how allergists test, common triggers and when to get urgent care.
excerpt: Yes, people can be allergic to cannabis. Here is how reactions show up, what allergists look for, the usual triggers and when a reaction needs emergency care.
keyTakeaways: Cannabis allergy is real, but nobody knows yet how common it is.
Reactions follow the exposure: hay-fever symptoms from smoke or pollen, hives or rashes from touching the plant, and serious reactions, including anaphylaxis, most often after eating hemp seed.
The recognized cannabis allergens are plant proteins, not THC or CBD.
There is no standardized commercial test, so an allergist relies on your history plus specialized skin or blood tests.
Avoidance is the only proven approach. Trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or fainting means calling 911.
body:
Yes, you can be allergic to cannabis. A cannabis allergy is your immune system overreacting to proteins in the plant. It can look like hay fever, a rash after handling flower or, in some people, a severe reaction called anaphylaxis. Allergists recognize it, but the research is still young. Here's what's known about symptoms, triggers and testing, and when to get emergency care.

## Is Cannabis Allergy Real, and How Common Is It?

It's real. Doctors first described allergic reactions to cannabis about 50 years ago. In 2022, an international consensus of allergists concluded that cannabis can cause both immediate allergic reactions and delayed skin reactions.

How common it is remains an open question. A 2023 review says the true prevalence still isn't known. One Spanish allergy clinic found clinically relevant cannabis sensitization in about 0.4% of patients seen for breathing or skin symptoms, but clinic patients aren't the general public. Reviewers expect more cases as legal use grows, though no study has measured that yet.

## Symptoms by Exposure

Reactions depend mostly on how you came into contact with the plant. Immediate reactions usually start within 30 minutes.

| How you were exposed | What a reaction can look like |
|---|---|
| Breathing in smoke, vapor or pollen | Sneezing, runny or stuffy nose, itchy or watery eyes, coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath |
| Touching flower or leaves | Itching, hives, redness, swelling under the skin (angioedema), or a rash that appears later |
| Eating edibles, cannabis tea or hemp seed | Hives, swelling and breathing symptoms, and sometimes anaphylaxis |

Some effects of cannabis itself, like red eyes, a racing heart and anxiety, aren't allergy. If symptoms are severe, get help first and sort out the cause later.

## Severe Reactions: Warning Signs of Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis is a whole-body reaction that can be life-threatening. A 2023 review reports that up to 20% of people with cannabis allergy have had one. It usually develops within seconds or minutes. Watch for:

- Trouble breathing, wheezing or high-pitched breathing sounds
- Swelling of the face, eyes or tongue, or trouble swallowing
- Hives, itching or redness of the skin
- Chest tightness, a pounding heartbeat, dizziness or fainting
- Nausea, vomiting, belly pain or slurred speech

Call 911 right away. If the person has an epinephrine auto-injector or nasal epinephrine, help them use it. Have them lie flat with their feet raised unless they're vomiting or injured, and give nothing by mouth if breathing is hard. Not sure whether it's an allergy or too much THC? Call anyway.

## How Allergists Diagnose It

The 2022 consensus calls your history the most important test, so be specific about how and when you were exposed. Be open, too: Michigan adults 21 and up can use cannabis legally, and our [cannabis FAQ](/faq/) covers the basics.

No standardized commercial cannabis extract exists, so testing varies by clinic:

- **Prick-to-prick skin tests** that use a bud, leaf or seed
- **Blood tests for IgE to hemp,** which catch most true cases but are often positive in people with pollen allergies who tolerate cannabis. As of a 2023 review, only a research test and one multi-allergen panel offered them.
- **Component tests** for single proteins such as Can s 3, most useful in Europe
- **Basophil activation tests,** offered mainly by specialized centers

Smoking or eating challenges aren't part of standard testing. If every test comes back negative, an allergy is unlikely.

## Common Triggers

- **Pollen.** Male plants shed it, and people living near hemp fields can get hay-fever-style symptoms.
- **Plant proteins.** All four officially recognized cannabis allergens are proteins, named Can s 2 through Can s 5.
- **Smoke.** Doctors have reported cannabis allergy from secondhand smoke at home.
- **Mold.** In people sensitive to mold, moldy cannabis can cause symptoms that look like cannabis allergy. Our [guide to storing cannabis](/blog/how-to-store-marijuana/) covers keeping flower dry.
- **Hemp seed.** Eating the seeds has caused serious reactions.
- **Cross-reacting foods.** Can s 3 resembles proteins in tomato, peach, hazelnut, citrus and other produce, so some people react to those too. As of a 2023 review, these food reactions had been reported only in Europe.
- **Terpenes.** They aren't recognized cannabis allergens, though some can bother skin (more below).

## Avoidance and Prevention, Including at Work

Prevention mostly means distance. Stop using cannabis until you've seen an allergist, step away from smoke and vapor, read food labels for hidden hemp seed, and wear gloves if you must handle plants.

Work exposure matters too. A 2025 study used surveillance data from California, Massachusetts, Michigan and Washington. It found 30 cases of work-related asthma in the legal cannabis industry through 2023, including two deaths. Plant material, almost all of it cannabis dust or plant matter, was the exposure reported most often, and 69% of the workers were in indoor cultivation or processing. If you work around cannabis and develop new or worse breathing symptoms, tell your doctor about your job and raise it with your employer. Protective equipment, ventilation and dust controls may lower the risk.

## Treatment Means Avoidance and Medical Care

No product fixes a cannabis allergy, and avoidance is the only proven approach. When contact can't be avoided, allergists manage symptoms as they would for other allergies. That may mean non-drowsy antihistamines, steroid nasal sprays, inhaled steroids or allergy eye drops. Anyone who has had anaphylaxis should carry epinephrine auto-injectors. Allergy shots for cannabis remain experimental.

Don't test your limits by switching products or trying smaller amounts. If you're a registered medical patient, bring the reaction up with your certifying physician; our [patient guide](/patient-guide/) explains Michigan's medical program.

## Questions About Smell, Cannabinoids and Terpenes

**The smell.** The allergens identified so far are proteins, while the smell comes from airborne aroma compounds. Secondhand smoke is different, since case reports tie it to allergic reactions. If the smell seems to set you off, an allergist can separate allergy from irritation.

**THC and CBD.** Neither is a recognized allergen. All four recognized cannabis allergens are plant proteins, so a so-called THC allergy is, as far as research shows, a reaction to the plant.

**Terpenes.** Limonene and linalool are among the main terpenes in cannabis and part of its aroma, and our [terpene guide](/blog/what-are-cannabis-terpenes/) explains how. They aren't cannabis allergens. Both are common fragrance ingredients, though, and once air oxidizes them they often trigger positive patch-test reactions in people with dermatitis. If scented products already irritate your skin, tell your allergist.

## The Bottom Line

Suspect a cannabis allergy? Stop using cannabis and see a board-certified allergist, who can sort out cannabis from pollen, mold or food triggers. Call 911 for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or fainting.

faq.a: Yes. Case reports describe cannabis allergy from breathing secondhand smoke at home, so people who don't use cannabis can react too. If someone nearby is smoking and you start sneezing, wheezing or itching, move to fresh air. If it keeps happening, an allergist can tell you whether cannabis is the cause. Anyone with asthma should take new breathing symptoms seriously and talk with their doctor.

faq.q: What does a cannabis skin reaction look like?
faq.a: It depends on the type. An immediate reaction shows up soon after contact as itching, redness, hives or swelling where the plant touched you. A delayed reaction, allergic contact dermatitis, can appear later as an itchy red rash and has been reported in people who handle or harvest plants. Wash the area and see a clinician if it spreads or lingers. Swelling of the face, lips or tongue is an emergency.

faq.q: Can hemp seeds cause an allergic reaction?
faq.a: Yes. Eating hemp seed is the exposure most often linked to anaphylaxis in people with cannabis allergy, and hemp seed can be hidden in foods and drinks. In one case series, most people who reacted to hemp seed also used cannabis, but 27% did not. If you have reacted to cannabis, ask your allergist whether to avoid hemp seed products too.
